extracted.intended_audience: historians of science, mathematicians interested in history, and educated general readers reading critiques of historical mathematical and scientific writings
extracted.subtask_description: Critical/historical commentary on mathematical and scientific writings (18th–19th century), identifying what makes historical accounts or scientific theories credible or fallacious. Emphasises historiographical standards, mathematical reasoning checks, and institutional responses to perpetual false claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge dependence on others / indicate when relying on secondary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Montucla is an admirable historian when he is writing from his own direct knowledge: it is a sad pity that he did not tell us when he was depending on others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historians should explicitly state when parts of their narrative are drawn from others rather than from their own direct knowledge; failure to do so reduces the trustworthiness of portions of a work (De Morgan: 'We are not to trust a quarter of his book').

rubrics_metrics.name: Base historical accounts on contemporary documents / primary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Delambre created a strong reaction ... in favor of history founded on contemporary documents, which early astronomy cannot furnish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer histories grounded in contemporary (primary) documents; where primary evidence is lacking, be cautious about grand claims regarding antiquity or origins. Delambre's reaction is cited as corrective to extravagant reconstructions based on insufficient documentary support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide adequate bibliographical descriptions and candid attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Montucla was nothing of a bibliographer, and his descriptions of books in the first edition were insufficient ... Montucla took it with great good humor, tried to mend, and, in his second edition, wished his critic had lived to see the vernis de bibliographe which he had given himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bibliographical entries should be sufficiently detailed and candid about sources and editions. Authors should respond to bibliographical criticism by improving descriptions rather than leaving gaps that mislead readers about provenance or authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test mathematical/general claims in extreme cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical truth is true in its extreme cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating mathematical or general propositions, check extreme or pathological cases to expose errors in supposed 'universal' rules (example: Weyman Lee's annuity rule gives absurd results when half the population is immortal). Extreme-case testing is a reliable method to falsify flawed general assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct valuation of life annuities: decompose into contingent payments
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole is the sum of all its parts ... All the difference between buying the whole from one office and buying all the separate contingent payments at different offices, is immaterial to calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value a life annuity by summing the present values of each contingent payment (i.e., treat each payment as separate contingent contract), rather than by substituting an 'average life' term or expectation as a single certain annuity — Lee's method of charging value by an even-chance term is mathematically erroneous (illustrated by a thousand-person extreme example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirm theories by deducing results that accord with later observations
rubrics_metrics.description: He, and many of his stamp, have not the least idea of the confirmation of a theory by accordance of deduced results with observation posterior to the theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A scientific theory gains credibility when specific consequences are deduced from it and those consequences are borne out by observations made after the theory was proposed. Mere verbal or speculative plausibility is insufficient; empirical confirmation of predictions is essential (counterexample given: Lovett's ether speculations lack such confirmation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret historical scientific terminology in its intended sense; avoid over-attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader should remember that the word attraction, as used by Newton and the best of his followers, only meant a 'drawing towards', without any implication as to the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing historical scientific texts, interpret key technical terms in the sense the original author intended, and avoid attributing stronger metaphysical or causal claims to them than they claimed. Beware anachronistically reading modern meanings into historical usage (example: Newton's cautious use of 'attraction').

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions may refuse to examine repeatedly fallacious or hopeless claims (institutional scope control)
rubrics_metrics.description: The French Academy of Sciences came to the determination not to examine any more quadratures or kindred problems. The Royal Society followed the same course ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learned bodies can enforce quality control by refusing to examine claims that have been repeatedly discredited or are manifestly untenable (e.g., persistent circle-squaring proposals). Such refusals are pragmatic measures to protect resources and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sweeping omniscience; support broad claims with named persons/documents
rubrics_metrics.description: It is all about l'homme ... not one opinion of any other man is referred to, in the way of agreement or of opposition. Not even a town is mentioned: there is nothing which brings a capital letter into the middle of a sentence ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors making broad philosophical or scientific assertions should ground their arguments in concrete examples, named authorities, or documented evidence. Sweeping generalities without references make works unconvincing and unreadable (De Morgan's criticism of Saint-Martin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deceptive bibliographic/publishing tricks to manufacture appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The book was printed at Lyons, but it was a trick of French authors to pretend to be afraid of prosecution: it made a book look wicked-like to have a feigned place of printing, and stimulated readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately falsifying printing locations or other bibliographic data to create a spurious aura of controversy or danger is a questionable practice and undermines scholarly trustworthiness; transparency about publication details is the better course.
